column2: Industries are like links in a chain: oil, gas and iron ore, then steel and petrochemicals, then cars, home appliances and food.
One link’s selling price is the next link’s cost.
So a supplier’s sales report shows early whether its customer will make more profit or less.
If the price of flour goes up, a few days later the bakery’s profit falls; the flour price is early news of the bakery’s profit.
Industries are linked like a chain
Who sets the product’s price? The world market, the commodity exchange, the government, or the free domestic market?
What is the biggest cost, and who controls its price?
How much capacity does the factory have and what percentage of it is working?
What stops competitors coming in? A licence, its own mine, a brand, a distribution network.
Before buying a taxi service you ask: who sets the fares, what petrol costs, how many hours the cars work, and how hard it is for a rival to start up.
When a company’s profit is a small part of its sales, a small price change shakes profit a lot.
In this card’s example the company makes 30% of its sales as profit; if the product price falls 10%, its profit falls by about a third.
The smaller the profit per unit, the bigger the risk. Do this calculation for every company you own.
A shop that sells 100 and has 70 of costs makes 30 profit. If it has to sell for 90, its profit becomes 20: 10% less in sales, 33% less profit.
After a capital increase, the share price is adjusted down because there are more shares.
For example, price 5,000 and one new share for each share at 1,000 rials: (5,000 + 1,000) ÷ 2 = 3,000. If the new share is free (from retained earnings): 2,500.
On the adjustment day your wealth doesn’t change; you just have more shares. “A capital increase means profit” is a false belief.
If you cut a cake into 8 slices instead of 4, you have 8 slices but the same amount of cake.
A capital increase doesn’t make more money
The main question: how much profit does the money shareholders just put in make?
If the new project gives a return above the share’s current return and above the risk-free return, and managers have a good record of delivering, it has created value.
If the money is only spent on paying off debt or losses, everyone’s share gets smaller without more profit coming.
If you neither sell your right nor pay for it, it’s sold for you and the money may arrive late.
If you and your partner each put another 10 million into the shop and the shop only pays off its debts, your monthly profit doesn’t grow; but if it opens a busy second branch, it does.
A right means first claim to buy the new shares; you only get it when the capital increase comes from shareholders’ fresh money.
If the capital increase comes from retained earnings, you get “bonus shares” instead and pay nothing.
Like old neighbours in a building getting first claim to buy a new flat: if they don’t want it, they can sell that right to someone else.
Pass shares through a five-stage funnel:
1. Loss-making companies, companies with heavy losses, and those whose report the auditor rejected are removed. 2. The company’s main work made a profit in most years and made real cash.
3. Bank debt is low. 4. The price is sensible: you get your money back in about 4 to 5 years and the return beats Akhza.
5. There’s a clear reason for value to rise: a new project, a high dividend, or a price far below the value of its assets.
Like hiring: first incomplete CVs are set aside, then work experience, then the interview, then the salary asked for, and finally what new thing they bring to the team.
The stock selection funnel
Hold 8 to 15 companies: fewer means one mistake can finish you; more means you can’t keep up with them all.
Each company at most 10 to 15% of your money, and each industry at most 25 to 30%.
Have both companies that sell in dollars and domestic ones, and keep part of your assets in gold or silver.
Review the weights every 3 or 6 months, not every day.
You don’t put all your eggs in one basket; but you don’t buy so many baskets that you can’t carry them all either.
Only sell for one of these three reasons, which you wrote down in advance:
1. The reason you bought is gone; for example, the company’s lasting profit has fallen.
2. The price has risen so far that it’s now expensive.
3. You’ve found a much better option. A price fall alone is no reason to sell.
You don’t sell a home you’re comfortable in because prices in the area dipped for a month; if the building cracks, you do.
Net profit grew but profit from the main work didn’t; so the growth came from somewhere else.
Companies close to the main owner owe the company more every year, and dividends are settled against these debts instead of in cash.
Real cash is less than half of profit for several years; or the company pays out a lot of profit while its borrowing rises fast.
The auditor raises the same problems every year, or the company keeps changing auditors and reports late.
A friend who says they’re doing great but borrows from you every month probably isn’t doing great.
Warning bells (1)
Sales money goes up but the number of units sold has been falling for months; or it keeps producing more than it sells.
It sells to its own group’s companies below the market price.
It keeps taking fresh money from shareholders for projects that never start running.
This year’s profit is from selling assets or the dollar, but the market prices it like normal profit; or the price moves on strange volume before important news.
If a shopkeeper gives goods to their own relatives at half price, the shop’s profit falls; the partners should know.
